text:
The Trump administration is providing federal funds to support coal plants, including one in Arizona that previously received money to go coal-free.

Energy experts argue that propping up aging coal plants is costly for both ratepayers and the environment.

Despite a national trend of retiring coal plants, some utilities are delaying their clean energy goals.

Two years ago an Arizona power plant received hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding to invest in renewable energy and go coal-free by 2028. Now, under a different presidential administration it’s getting more money — this time in support of coal.

The Apache Generating Station planned to retire coal by the end of next year, but on June 4 it was granted nearly $21 million in exchange for maintaining and updating the coal turbine, which is also capable of running on natural gas.

It isn’t alone. The Department of Energy announced plans to dole out $425 million to 12 existing coal facilities across the country that applied for funding made available under the Defense Production Act.

At a time when energy experts say the nation should be moving away from coal, President Donald Trump is invoking a war-time provision to revive coal as it’s phased out in favor of cheaper, cleaner alternatives.

The announcement is the latest in his coal crusade. Since Trump took office last January, his administration has ordered five coal plants to continue operating past their retirement dates, opened 13 million acres of public lands to coal mining, rolled back air quality standards for coal-fired power plants and introduced a new spokesperson for its energy dominance agenda — “Coalie,” a cartoonified lump of coal wearing a miner’s hard hat and a bashful smile.

Trump said the recent investment will save Americans billions. But experts warn that keeping coal alive could end up costing ratepayers – and the environment — a lot more.

Coal power plant retirements have been a long time coming, said Amanda Ormond, Executive Director for the Just Energy Transition Center at Arizona State University.

Over the last decade, coal plants have retired at a higher rate than other kinds of power plants, according to the Energy Information Administration.

Incentivizing them to stay open is like pushing a rock uphill, Ormond said.

Without continued assistance, utilities won’t be able to afford to keep their coal turbines running, said Ted Kelly, the director and lead counsel of U.S. clean energy for the Environmental Defense Fund. The administration's new federal funding is trying to fill a “gaping wound” of increasing costs.

Coal, hard cash

Arizona Electric Power Cooperative’s Apache Generating Station is one of three power plants in the state still using coal. Over the last few years, Arizona’s largest utility companies have started moving away from coal-powered generation — much to the president’s chagrin.

Last spring, Arizona Public Service closed its Cholla coal plant in Navajo County. The decision garnered immediate backlash from state lawmakers and from Trump, who instructed Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright to save the power plant.

"We're going to have that plant opening and burning the clean coal, beautiful clean coal, in a very short period of time,” the president said last April after signing executive orders keeping a host of other coal plants on life support. Despite the federal pressure, the Cholla plant has remained closed.

Coal generation has grown costly, Kelly said. Since 2020, prices for the fuel have been on the rise, and over the last two decades demand has been on the decline. Coal turbines are some of the oldest in the country — the Apache Generating Station’s is 47 years old — making them costly to maintain.

A decade ago, coal accounted for 38% of power generation in Arizona. Now, it only makes up 8%, according to a 2024 estimate by the Energy Information Administration. Instead, 45% of the state’s power comes from gas and 19% comes from renewables like solar and wind.

“In general, coal plants retire because they aren’t cost-effective compared to the new stuff,” Ormond said.

Remaining open would’ve cost the Cholla plant nearly $2 billion in upgrades and maintenance, according to the Arizona Corporation Commission. It closed in part to avoid lawsuits with the Environmental Protection Agency.

In 2024, the EPA updated air quality standards for coal and oil-fired power plants under the Clean Air Act, which meant reigning in emissions of harmful heavy metals like mercury by 2027. For some plants, that meant investing in new pollution capture equipment — a cost often more expensive than retiring coal turbines altogether or transitioning them to natural gas.

In March, the state approved plans for Salt River Project and Tucson Electric Power to convert their coal turbines to gas. In 2023, TEP announced that it would shift away from coal by the end of the decade. The company cited rising fuel costs, mine closures and environmental regulations in a press release last summer.

Keeping the coal turbines running would’ve taken over $450 million in upgrades to meet EPA guidelines, according to the Arizona Corporation Commission. Converting the turbines from coal to gas will cost $170 million.

The Apache Generation Station evaded the expenses associated with the new emissions rule, even while continuing to operate. Last April, it was one of 66 coal-burning facilities that applied for and received exemptions from the updated federal air pollution standards.

The plant’s coal turbine nearly tripled the amount of mercury it emitted from 2024 to 2025 — even though its operating hours decreased, according to EPA data.

In February, the agency finalized a rollback of the 2024 emissions rule for all oil and coal-fired power plants.

“The Biden-Harris Administration’s anti-coal regulations sought to regulate out of existence this vital sector of our energy economy. If implemented, these actions would have destroyed reliable American energy,” EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said in a press release.

The administration's reversal might make coal plants marginally less expensive. But it does so at the cost of the environment, Kelly said.

“Coal power plants have really severe air quality consequences,” he said. For local communities they can exacerbate asthma, contribute to heart problems and lead to premature deaths.

The costs of keeping coal plants open

Reviving coal doesn’t just cost utility companies and the environment, in many cases it takes a toll on ratepayers’ wallets.

When the Arizona Corporation Commission approved TEP’s plans to convert their turbines in March, it noted that the costs associated with keeping them running on coal — $450 million — would’ve been passed onto ratepayers.

Apart from the nearly $21 million the power co-op is set to receive from the Department of Energy, it will have to match another $32 million in cost-sharing funds.

The funding includes a cost-sharing requirement to make sure the recipients have a stake in the long-term success of the project, a department spokesperson said in an email. Typically, that money comes from power plant owners and operators.

Arizona Electric Power Co-op told The Republic that it’s in discussions with the department regarding that requirement. The utility said the $21 million in federal funding will be used to improve efficiency and reduce long-term maintenance costs at the coal turbine, which will save money and for AEPCO members and consumers.

It did not respond to questions on how the cost-matched funds will be raised or if those costs will fall to ratepayers.

The utility is “evaluating all options,” said Caryolyn Turner, the company’s director of communications in an email.

Local representatives have praised the department’s announcement.

"I have long supported an all-of-the-above approach to energy because it is the best way to strengthen our energy security, lower costs, and meet the needs of growing communities,” said U.S. Rep. Juan Ciscomani of Arizona’s 6th Congressional District in a June 4 press release.

But an “all-of-the-above approach” that includes coal doesn’t necessarily amount to affordability for ratepayers.

“As we’ve seen with these coal plants kept open by the Trump administration, they've really increased electric costs in the area,” Kelly said.

One of the five power plants that the Department of Energy included in its directive last year has lost $180 million by continuing to operate. The utility that owns that Michigan power plant is looking to residents of 11 states to shoulder that cost.

In May, Michigan, Minnesota and Illinois, along with nine non-profit groups, argued to overturn the department's directive in a D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. The case will have implications for the four other coal plants ordered to keep running.

Back-tracking on renewable energy?

Two years ago, Arizona Electric Power Co-op shared big plans for its renewable energy transition.

The utility was granted $485 million in “Empowering Rural America” funds from the U.S. Department of Agriculture under Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act. It planned to use the money to build 800 megawatts in renewable energy projects and be coal-free by 2028.

Some of those projects have already come to fruition. In April, the Co-op announced the completion of a 295 MW solar field in Cochise. Another 400 MW solar project is also in the works, Turner said in an email.

But Ormond wonders what the new federal money could mean for the future of coal at the utility. AEPCO did not respond to questions from The Republic about whether the funding could extend the life of the coal turbine past its planned retirement date.

“AEPCO is committed to fulfilling all grant obligations under its New ERA application, including the commitment to reduce the emissions of its generation portfolio 70% by 2031. AEPCO’s projected 2031 resource mix contains over 60% renewable resources, and includes solar, battery storage, and hydropower generation,” Turner said in an email.

Other utilities in Arizona are back-tracking on previous clean energy commitments.

Last year, APS pushed its goal to be coal-free by 2031. Now, the company plans to close its remaining Four Corners coal plant in 2038 at the latest, a spokesperson for the utility told The Republic in August.

In New Mexico, a Navajo mine that supplies coal to the Four Corners plant announced plans during a January meeting to expand and continue operations 110 years in the future — even though the power plant is slated for closure in the next 14.

“We need to be investing in the cleanest, most cost-effective technology,” Ormond said, like solar and wind.

“Coal is a resource of the past, " she said. “This takes our energy system backwards.”

name: Texas Environment
title: Manufacturers and Data Centers Compete for Megawatts - Environment+Energy Leader
description:
That volume of interest reflects a grid trying to catch up to demand growth that data centers and other large loads created, not a queue built with industrial expansion in mind.
For manufacturers, the practical takeaway is that the fast lane exists, but it was not built for them.
It is tempting to read all of this as data centers beating manufacturers to the punch, but that framing gives utilities more discretion than they actually have.
High-voltage transformer lead times that ran 24 to 30 months before 2020 now stretch as long as five years, driven largely by the same data center buildout competing for grid capacity.
Regional power markets are pricing in data center demand faster than they can build supply to match it, and every other large electricity user in that market pays the difference.
text:
Power is now the first constraint checked, and in a growing number of regions, manufacturers are discovering that the capacity they assumed would be available has already been claimed by a data center campus down the road. The competition is not hypothetical. It shows up in interconnection queues, transformer order books, and utility large-load dockets across the country.

The scale of the mismatch is easiest to see in PJM, the regional grid operator spanning 13 states and Washington, D.C. Its most recent interconnection cycle drew more than 800 project applications totaling roughly 220 gigawatts (GW) of proposed generation, according to PJM Inside Lines. That volume of interest reflects a grid trying to catch up to demand growth that data centers and other large loads created, not a queue built with industrial expansion in mind. Getting into that queue is only the first hurdle. RMI, the clean energy research organization formerly known as Rocky Mountain Institute, found that the average timeline from interconnection application to commercial operation in PJM has stretched from under two years in 2008 to more than eight years by 2025, and that 74% of the 294 GW PJM has studied since 2020 withdrew before ever reaching service.

PJM's Reopened Queue Favors Whoever Applied First, Not Whoever Needs Power Most

PJM shifted in 2022 from a first-come, first-served model to a first-ready, first-served process, screening out speculative projects before they can occupy queue positions that industrial developers might otherwise use. The Electric Power Supply Association reports that its member generators have announced more than 12 GW of new capacity in PJM since mid-2024 through new builds, uprates, and delayed retirements, a response to the shortage that is real but slow relative to the pace of large-load additions. A manufacturer weighing a multi-year capital project now has to ask whether its timeline can survive a queue that was reformed for reliability, not for speed. In most cases, the honest answer is no.

The reform also introduced the Expedited Interconnection Track, a parallel pathway for large, advanced projects that can demonstrate full site control and post a readiness deposit of $15,000 per megawatt. PJM caps that track at ten approved projects per year, and it was built with large generation resources in mind, not industrial facilities trying to secure delivery capacity. For manufacturers, the practical takeaway is that the fast lane exists, but it was not built for them.

Utilities Don't Choose Winners. They Allocate Scarcity.

It is tempting to read all of this as data centers beating manufacturers to the punch, but that framing gives utilities more discretion than they actually have. A utility studying an interconnection request is not weighing whether a hyperscaler's mission matters more than a factory's. It is checking whether the applicant already has a signed load contract and a deposit on file, whether the engineering study has progressed far enough that construction could realistically start, and whether the local transmission system has room left to carry the additional draw. State commissions and FERC add their own sign-off on top of that. Data center developers tend to clear that bar faster, not because utilities favor them, but because they walk in with the offtake agreement signed, the deposit funded, and an engineering team that has run this exact process dozens of times before.

That distinction matters for how executives should read the competition. The system is not biased against industrial users. It is simply allocating a finite resource to whichever applicant proves readiness first, and readiness has become a function of capital and process discipline rather than industry type. A manufacturer that treats utility engagement as a late-stage formality will keep losing that race to whoever treats it as a parallel workstream from day one, regardless of what gets built next door.

Transformer Backlogs Are Turning Site Selection Into a Manufacturing Supply Chain Problem

Even a manufacturer with an approved interconnection agreement can be stalled by hardware. High-voltage transformer lead times that ran 24 to 30 months before 2020 now stretch as long as five years, driven largely by the same data center buildout competing for grid capacity. Eaton, Vertiv, and Schneider Electric have all announced new manufacturing capacity for grid equipment, but new factories take years to reach full output, meaning the shortage will outlast most current expansion plans. A facility that clears its interconnection study can still sit dark for a year or more waiting on the switchgear needed to actually accept power. The bottleneck has effectively migrated from the substation to the factory floor of the companies that build substations.

ERCOT and PJM Show the Same Squeeze Playing Out Differently

In Texas, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) projects peak summer demand could reach approximately 145 GW by 2031, up from 85 GW in 2024, according to research compiled by Harvard's Belfer Center. Much of that growth traces back to the Dallas-Fort Worth data center corridor, drawn by competitive power prices and fast interconnection speeds that are now disappearing as the queue fills. Texas manufacturers considering expansion in the same corridor are effectively competing against the workload that made the region attractive in the first place. PJM's capacity market tells a parallel story: its most recent auction procured roughly 145,777 megawatts (MW), falling about 6.6 GW short of the reliability target and pushing capacity prices to a record. Both grids are telling the same story from different angles. Regional power markets are pricing in data center demand faster than they can build supply to match it, and every other large electricity user in that market pays the difference.

When the Queue Won't Move, Manufacturers Are Starting to Build Their Own Power

Facing years-long wait times, some industrial operators are adopting a strategy data center developers pioneered: generating power on site rather than waiting for the grid. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) issued emergency orders in January and May 2026 directing utilities to keep aging plants running through peak demand periods, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright has pointed to roughly 35 GW of underused backup generation nationally that could be called on during grid stress. That figure is a reminder that behind-the-meter capacity, long treated as an emergency reserve, is becoming a primary planning tool for any large power user willing to invest in it upfront. For manufacturers without a hyperscaler's balance sheet, that investment is a harder call, but it is increasingly the only way to control a timeline the grid no longer controls for them.

In addition to asking the court to block the permit, the motion requests that it rescind the Corps’ No Effects determination.
text:
Residents of Louisiana’s River Parishes today asked a federal court to block an expedited federal permit for a construction project that threatens the gravesites of their enslaved ancestors. The plaintiffs – Rural Roots Louisiana, Mount Triumph Baptist Church, and Pastor Harry Joseph, Jr. – seek a temporary restraining order that would enjoin the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers from issuing an expedited permit to CF Industries, which aims to build an ammonia factory on former plantation land in the historic predominantly Black community of Modeste, until the court holds a hearing. Administration officials have boasted that the Army Corps had moved the permit at “Trump speed.”

The ammonia factory would be part of a proposed “RiverPlex MegaPark,” a 17,000-acre industrial development that would displace hundreds of people and compound the already severe health risks for thousands of residents in the heart of Cancer Alley. Because the ammonia factory would impact wetlands, it requires a permit from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. The plaintiffs sued the Corps in April, demanding that it issue a cease-a-desist order to CF Industries to halt the construction activities taking place prior to the issuance of a final permit. The temporary restraining order would maintain the status quo while the lawsuit proceeds.

“Every day, we see dump trucks, bulldozers, and heavy equipment cut through our community in a rush to build this new plant,” said Twila Collins, a Modeste resident who also submitted a declaration in support of the temporary restraining order. “I’ve even had contractors show up uninvited on my property. If they have no respect for those of us who live here, it’s hard to believe they will have any respect for our ancestors buried here.”

“For decades, this area was protected as conservation land with historic significance, sacred burial sites, and the families who have called it home for generations,” said Ashley Gaignard, founder of Rural Roots Louisiana. “We are deeply concerned that those protections are being dismantled to make way for heavy industry in the middle of Black residential communities. Our concerns have been dismissed while state leaders characterize community opposition as an obstacle to economic development. Industry should never come at the expense of our history, our health, or our right to have a meaningful voice in decisions that affect our future. We refuse to accept a future where our ancestors’ legacy is erased and our air and water are treated as expendable. Our communities deserve investment that protects both people and the places they have cherished for generations.”

Elsewhere in Cancer Alley, corporations have built – and are seeking to build – factories on land containing the gravesites of people who were forced to work and die on plantations. The destruction of these sacred sites has caused trauma for descendants in the area, which is precisely what the plaintiffs are experiencing as they witness the disruption of grounds they know are home to the final resting places of their enslaved ancestors. Absent injunctive relief, the Corps will soon issue the permit, inflicting irreversible harm on the plaintiffs.

“The Corps of Engineers needs to do their job and find the gravesites we know are on that property,” said Harry Joseph, Jr., a local resident and pastor of Mount Triumph Baptist Church. “That is our history and those are our ancestors and we want to know where they are and what the Corps is going to do to protect them.”

The National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) requires federal agencies to undertake a review of the impact of their decisions on historical properties. Guidance from the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, which advises agencies on NHPA compliance, says they must treat human remains with respect and instructs them to consider the legacy of slavery. The review process must include a consultation with impacted parties. Although the Corps granted Rural Roots “consulting party status,” it did not actually consult with the group before issuing its final determination that the construction would have no adverse effects on historic properties.

“Corporations profiting from the construction of these polluting facilities should not be allowed to bulldoze the rights, history, and health of community members in Modeste,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. “Instead of following the law, state and federal officials are fast-tracking approvals for the Riverplex MegaPark, prioritizing polluter profits over the health and wellbeing of the people.”

Moreover, the plaintiffs argue that the Thirteenth Amendment – which was intended to abolish slavery and its remnants, or “badges and incidents” – requires the Corps to locate and protect the gravesites likely situated on the land prior to allowing any construction on such sites. The burial grounds that hold the remains of people who perished in bondage are clear remnants of slavery.

“On the eve of the 250th anniversary of this country, people from this community are trying desperately to protect their history from erasure and the graves of enslaved ancestors from corporate greed aided by the misdirection and complicity of federal officials,” said Pam Spees, a senior staff attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights.

The motion for a temporary restraining order was filed on the plaintiffs’ behalf by the Center for Constitutional Rights, the Environmental Integrity Project, and Louisiana attorney William P. Quigley. In addition to asking the court to block the permit, the motion requests that it rescind the Corps’ No Effects determination.

For more information, visit the Center for Constitutional Rights case page.

text:
Concrete is the world’s most widely used construction material and remains essential to modern infrastructure. The increasing global population and rapid urbanization, particularly in developing countries, have contributed to a rising demand for concrete. For example, from 1990 to 2020, global production of concrete and mortar increased approximately fourfold, reflecting its critical role in modern construction1,2. However, from a materials standpoint, traditional concrete production is energy-intensive, primarily due to the ordinary Portland cement (OPC) manufacturing process, which serves as the principal binder in concrete. This process has led to a significant rise in carbon emissions. The production of one ton of OPC typically requires approximately 1.2–1.3 tons of limestone and 0.3–0.4 tons of clay, resulting in carbon emissions on the order of 0.7–0.9 tons of CO2 per ton of cement3,4. These emissions from OPC production alone contribute to roughly 8% of global anthropogenic CO2 emissions, underscoring the urgency of mitigation efforts5,6. Although the transportation of concrete raw materials such as cement and aggregates also contributes to carbon emissions, its impact is relatively minor. At the concrete lifecycle scale, cement production remains the dominant source of emissions, whereas aggregate transportation generally contributes a much smaller share7,8. Therefore, mitigating the environmental impact of concrete production requires not only reducing the carbon footprint of cementitious materials, but also improving material efficiency through optimized structural design and aggregate grading.

To address this challenge, researchers and industry stakeholders have been exploring various strategies to reduce the carbon footprint of concrete. These strategies include the application of supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs)9 such as fly ash (FA)10, ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBFS)11, and silica fume (SF)12, which can partially replace OPC in concrete mixtures, thereby reducing CO2 emissions associated with OPC production. Meanwhile, the adoption of alternative binders, which can fully replace OPC, such as geopolymers and magnesia-based cements, offers a promising pathway for producing low-carbon concrete13,14,15,16. Furthermore, the recycling and reuse of construction waste generated from the demolition of buildings after decades or even centuries of service represent an effective and complementary strategy for lowering environmental impacts. Typically, old concrete is crushed and recycled as aggregate for new concrete, supporting the development of recycled aggregate concrete (RAC)17,18,19. While this approach can reduce the demand for virgin aggregates, its overall carbon benefit depends on factors such as aggregate quality and potential increases in cement content. Lastly, the concept of carbon sequestration in concrete has emerged as a possible solution for mitigating carbon emissions. This involves the use of materials that capture and store CO220,21,22. Technologies such as carbon mineralization23,24 and the use of biochar25,26,27 have shown potential to enhance the carbon sequestration capacity of concrete, although the net carbon benefit of biochar depends on system boundaries and alternative biomass utilization pathways.

While numerous researchers have extensively explored the technological roadmap for further achieving low-carbon concrete, most research has concentrated on a singular theme: analyzing the relationship between various concrete properties and the mix design. Early research on concrete followed three scientific paradigms: empiricism, theory, and computation28. Empirical approaches primarily relied on repeated experimentation and simple statistical or semi-analytical models to fit experimental data, such as code-based mix design methods (e.g., ACI, MC 2010, Eurocode) and empirical formulas reported in experimental studies. While these methods can be effective within tested conditions, they require substantial experimental efforts and often lack generalization capability, limiting their broader applicability. As cement chemistry advanced, researchers developed a deeper understanding of the physical and chemical processes involved in cement hydration29. By applying principles of hydration kinetics, thermodynamics, and related scientific laws, theoretical modeling has been used to elucidate the mechanisms governing the performance of cement-based materials, thereby reducing the need for extensive experimentation. Building on this, computational simulation represents a distinct but complementary paradigm, where advanced numerical tools such as HYMOSTRUC30, μic31, and CemHyd3D32, as well as atomistic approaches such as density-functional theory (DFT)33,34 and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations35,36,37, are primarily used to investigate hydration mechanisms and microstructural evolution in greater detail. While both paradigms rely on fundamental scientific laws, the key distinction lies in theoretical models emphasizing simplified analytical representations, whereas computational methods simulate these processes explicitly at multiple scales.

A review of the three paradigms for concrete analysis shows that they either demand extensive experimentation, require substantial computational resources, or are difficult to validate experimentally, largely due to the inherent complexity of concrete composition and the multitude of interacting physical and chemical factors. Consequently, empirical, semi-empirical, or theoretical models developed for concrete performance, while widely adopted in design codes for property prediction and structural design, are often limited in accuracy and generalizability due to their simplified assumptions. This is precisely where machine learning (ML)-based approaches hold promise for providing more reliable and scalable predictions38. While empirical and statistical models may benefit from larger datasets within a fixed problem domain, their predictive capability often deteriorates when extrapolated to new material systems or environmental conditions, owing to their simplified assumptions and limited adaptability. As a data-driven approach, ML addresses the challenges of analyzing large datasets and is thus regarded as the fourth paradigm of scientific discovery39. ML can efficiently and accurately predict various properties of concrete by uncovering the underlying correlations within data and accounting for the complex interactions among different constituents. For example, ML models have been successfully applied to predict compressive strength (CS) based on mixture proportions and curing conditions, optimize rheological properties for 3D-printable concretes40, and estimate durability indicators such as chloride penetration41 and carbonation depth42. By reducing the need for extensive trial-and-error experimentation and providing flexible data-driven modeling capabilities, ML has seen widespread adoption in concrete research in recent years.

Several recent reviews have examined the application of ML in cement and concrete. However, most of these works emphasize general trends and broad applications rather than providing a systematic comparison across different cementitious systems. Existing reviews have provided valuable insights into the application of machine learning for predicting properties such as strength and durability. Many of these studies focus on general trends or specific performance indicators, with comparatively less emphasis on distinguishing among different binder systems, such as OPC, alkali-activated materials, and blended cements. In addition, the connection between ML applications and carbon mitigation strategies is often discussed in a more case-specific context. As a result, the potential role of ML in supporting the transition toward low-carbon cementitious materials would benefit from a more systematic synthesis. This motivates the present work, which aims to provide a structured analysis linking ML applications with specific strategies for reducing the environmental impact of concrete.

Typically, the development of low-carbon concrete can be considered across four main directions: (i) reducing carbon emissions associated with cement clinker and aggregate production; (ii) incorporating SCMs and developing alternative binders; (iii) optimizing mix design to improve material efficiency while reducing experimental effort; and (iv) utilizing recycled aggregate concrete (RAC). In this context, this review examines the literature and discusses how ML can support low-carbon concrete development across these four directions (Fig. 1).

The goal of this review is to synthesize the current state of knowledge regarding the application of ML in the development of low-carbon concrete. By examining advances in cement production, mix design, and performance prediction, this review highlights the potential of ML in driving the construction industry toward more sustainable practices. Unlike existing reviews that mainly emphasize general property prediction, this work organizes recent studies according to four main directions and distinguishes ML applications across major cementitious systems. It also identifies current limitations and outlines future research directions for reducing the environmental impact of concrete and supporting progress toward net-zero construction.

Cement production is an energy-intensive process. Wet-process kilns historically required much higher thermal energy than dry-process systems, while modern clinker production is predominantly based on dry-process kilns, typically operating at about 3.3-3.4 GJ/t of clinker43. This substantial energy consumption significantly contributes to the overall energy footprint of concrete systems. Rotary kilns remain the most efficient and reliable method for converting large quantities of raw materials into cement clinker44,45,46. However, cement manufacturers face challenges in further optimizing clinker production due to uncertainties in the energy requirements of the process and the substantial investments needed for many energy-saving technologies. Developing accurate analytical models that predict energy consumption specific to product quality and facility processes could facilitate significant improvements in both energy efficiency and product quality control. Such improvements, when implemented at scale, could translate into substantial energy savings and CO2 reductions at the global level, given the large volume of clinker production.

The operation of a cement rotary kiln is highly complex, involving physical changes and chemical reactions in raw materials, fuel combustion, and heat transfer among these processes, which traditional control technologies struggle to manage accurately. Ali et al.47 addressed this challenge by developing and training a neural network that integrates quality control and process data to predict cement quality, thereby overcoming the limitations of the traditional stoichiometry-based Bogue’s model. By employing a feedforward neural network trained on two years of industrial production data, the model achieved significantly lower prediction errors for clinker mineral composition and enabled its integration into nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC). The results highlight that accurate prediction of clinker composition not only reduces the need for frequent laboratory testing and manual adjustments but also supports energy-efficient kiln operation, thereby contributing to lower CO2 emissions in cement production.

For the optimization of cement clinker production, Pan et al.48 employed a genetic algorithm (GA)-optimized neural network using key operational parameters, including raw meal feed rate and coal feeding rates to the rotary kiln and precalciner, to predict specific standard coal consumption. Their model achieved reliable predictive performance and identified optimized operating conditions that reduced coal consumption to approximately 80 kg standard coal per ton of clinker, demonstrating the potential of ML to improve energy efficiency and reduce fuel-related emissions in industrial practice.

In parallel, Gonçalves et al.49 integrated thermodynamic simulations with a deep learning (DL) model to optimize clinker phase composition, focusing on alite- and belite-rich systems. The DL model was used to identify optimal SiO2 and CaO contents required to achieve target C3S levels, with predictions closely matching thermodynamic calculations. The results highlighted the sensitivity of C3S formation to temperature and raw meal chemistry, and identified suitable lime saturation factor (LSF) ranges for producing alite- and belite-rich clinkers. This hybrid modeling approach illustrates how data-driven methods, when combined with physical principles, can support informed decision-making in clinker design and process optimization.

Cement manufacturing requires the extraction of substantial quantities of raw materials, which consumes significant fossil energy and results in considerable CO2 emissions. In recent years, the calcination process has garnered increased attention from the public and government, as it is the main cause of CO2 emissions within the cement industry50. To effectively manage the carbon produced during calcination, the cement manufacturing industry must develop improved methods for quantifying carbon emissions. Boakye et al.51 employed six ML algorithms to investigate two output parameters: the apparent degree of oxidation and the apparent degree of calcification. They found that the Gas outlet temperature of the third preheater stage was one of the variables with a strong correlation to CO2 emissions, while the control of kiln main drive speed was the second variable with the highest correlation to CO2. With this crucial insight, these two variables can be predetermined in the laboratory, necessitating the installation of key monitoring instruments during experiments to observe their real-time variations. Furthermore, optimizing kiln operations requires a comprehensive approach that simultaneously considers multiple parameters to minimize environmental impact52,53.

Given that current methods for cement carbon accounting require high-resolution data from numerous production-line processes and are therefore both labor-intensive and expensive, Zhou et al.54 investigated the potential of using ML to develop an Electricity-Carbon Coupling model. They utilized daily production line inventory and electricity consumption data from a cement factory in southern China as the basis for their study. Their in-depth analysis revealed a strong connection between electricity usage and total CO2 emissions in the cement production process. Notably, all six ML algorithms they tested were able to predict total CO2 emissions with high accuracy using electricity data. Predictions based on supply-side power data (R2 = 0.96) turned out to be more precise than those based on consumption-side power data (R2 = 0.87). With the growing adoption of second-generation dry-process cement production and waste heat recovery technologies in the industry, these innovative electricity-carbon models hold significant potential for broader application, offering a more straightforward and efficient approach to verifying carbon emissions in cement clinker production.

The inherent uncertainty in industrial processes often presents considerable challenges to the seamless operation and production control within the sector. To address this issue, Boukhari55 applied three algorithms, i.e., Deep Neural Network (DNN), Ant Colony Optimization-based artificial neural network (ACO-ANN), and Genetic Algorithm-based ANN (GA-ANN), to estimate the percentage of CO2 emissions generated during cement clinker production. Among these, DNN demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy for CO2 emissions. Furthermore, Usman et al.56 employed hybrid ML and optimization frameworks to predict multiple gaseous emissions (CO2, NOx, CO, and O2) and to identify the most influential process parameters using sensitivity analysis techniques. Their results consistently highlighted coal consumption as the dominant factor governing emission behavior, underscoring the central role of fuel management in emission mitigation strategies for cement plants.

Beyond emission prediction, recent studies have integrated ML with physics-based simulation tools to enhance process efficiency. Cui et al.57 combined computational fluid dynamics with advanced ML architectures to optimize combustion efficiency and material decomposition in cement calcination furnaces. This hybrid framework enabled accurate prediction of key process indicators and supported operational adjustments aimed at improving energy efficiency while reducing pollutant emissions. Collectively, these studies illustrate that embedding ML into process monitoring and optimization workflows provides a practical pathway for managing industrial uncertainty, improving energy efficiency, and reducing carbon emissions in cement manufacturing.

Supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs)

To minimize the use of OPC in concrete, SCMs such as industrial by-products, natural volcanic ash, and materials with pozzolanic or latent hydraulic properties are commonly used to partially replace cement9,58,59,60. Life-cycle assessment indicates that incorporating SCMs can significantly reduce the energy consumption of concrete systems and markedly lower CO2 emissions61. As a result, there is a growing need to thoroughly analyze the chemical properties of SCMs and the characteristics of cement-based materials containing SCMs after hydration. With the advanced capabilities of ML, it is now possible to accurately predict the performance of concrete by leveraging extensive data analysis, thereby contributing to a reduction in the carbon footprint of concrete systems.

Globally, approximately 600 million tonnes of coal ash are produced annually, with FA comprising about 500 million tonnes, or roughly 80% of this total10. As an industrial byproduct of coal combustion, FA can be utilized as a SCM in concrete, which not only facilitates its recycling but also reduces the demand for cement. In a thorough investigation, Song et al.62 evaluated multiple supervised ML models, including gene expression programming (GEP), ANNs, and DT, using experimental datasets with varying mix proportions. The results showed that ensemble-based approaches achieved higher prediction accuracy than individual learners. Likewise, Sevim et al.63 developed a novel prediction model to estimate the CS of mortar samples with varying properties using ML techniques. ANNs and Adaptive-Network Based Fuzzy Inference Systems (ANFIS) were employed to predict CS based on SiO2 + Al2O3 + Fe2O3 content, age, and FA replacement ratios. The results demonstrated that the GA-based ANFIS model outperformed traditional multi-linear regression (MLR), suggesting its potential for future studies on predicting mortar CS using chemical composition and FA content.

Blast furnace slag, a byproduct of pig iron production in blast furnaces, primarily consists of calcium along with various silicates and aluminosilicates. When this molten slag is rapidly quenched in water, it transforms into an amorphous, glassy material11. GGBFS is acknowledged as a highly reactive SCM, with its hydraulic activity largely dependent on the slag’s basicity—the higher the basicity, the greater its hydraulic activity when exposed to alkaline activators64,65,66. Previous studies have shown that replacing approximately 40% of OPC with GGBFS can reduce the overall carbon emissions of concrete by about 22% at comparable strength levels67. ML applications to GGBFS-containing systems further demonstrate reliable performance prediction across a wide range of mix designs. Rathakrishnan et al.68 reported that boosting-based ML algorithms, particularly the Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBR), achieved high predictive accuracy for CS in high-volume GGBFS concrete. In parallel, other studies extended ML approaches to fracture-related properties, identifying key geometric and loading parameters governing fracture toughness69. These findings highlight the versatility of ML in modeling both strength and fracture behavior in slag-blended systems.

In addition to FA and GGBFS, materials such as SF70,71, steel slag72,73,74, metakaolin75,76, rice husk ash77,78, and waste glass powder (WGP)79,80 can also serve as SCMs in OPC systems. These SCMs exhibit significant differences in their physical and chemical properties due to their varied origins. From a material standpoint, the chemical composition, particle size distribution, and calcination temperature of SCMs influence their reactivity within the OPC system. From a mix design perspective, the substitution rate of these SCMs relative to OPC also plays a critical role in determining the concrete’s various properties. To provide a comprehensive overview of recent research on using ML to predict the performance of concrete containing SCMs, Table 1 provides a systematic summary of recent ML applications for concrete incorporating various SCMs, highlighting commonly adopted algorithms, input parameters, predicted performance indicators, and sustainability-related outcomes. This consolidated overview reveals consistent trends across different SCM systems, notably the dominant influence of curing age, cement content, water-to-binder (w/b) ratio, and SCM replacement level on concrete performance, while also illustrating the potential of ML to support low-carbon concrete design through informed material selection.

Alternative binders

While the incorporation of SCMs can partially reduce the reliance on OPC, they are not capable of fully replacing it. This limitation can be addressed by alternative cementitious binders81,82. Some of the prominent alternative binders include alkali-activated materials (AAMs)/geopolymers, magnesia-based materials, and limestone calcined clay cement (LC3). These binders have been developed primarily with the goal of minimizing environmental impact. Upon hydration, some of these alternatives can produce clinker phases similar to those found in OPC, such as in AAMs and LC3, thereby providing the necessary mechanical strength to the concrete82,83,84. However, the reaction mechanisms in certain systems, particularly AAMs, differ substantially from that of OPC. In such cases, it is essential to conduct new, comprehensive studies on the reaction mechanisms and performance evolution specific to these systems.

Geopolymers are widely regarded as alternative cementitious binders to OPC85. The term “geopolymer” is often used to describe alkali-activated aluminosilicate binders, although its relationship to the broader class of AAMs is not always defined consistently in the literature. Geopolymers are materials produced by combining industrial waste (such as FA, GGBFS) or calcined minerals (like metakaolin) with alkaline activators86,87. Not only do geopolymers enable the complete recycling of industrial solid waste, but their simple preparation process also positions them as a highly promising advanced green cementitious system. The properties of geopolymers are influenced by several factors, including the physical and chemical characteristics of their precursors, the type of activator used, and the environmental temperature. Common activators include NaOH, KOH, and Na2SiO385,88. Precursors can be classified into three categories based on their calcium content: high calcium (e.g., GGBFS), low calcium (e.g., class F FA), and calcium-free (e.g., metakaolin)89.

Beyond geopolymers, magnesia-based materials have garnered significant attention for their low-carbon attributes, primarily because the calcination temperature of their main raw material, MgO, is substantially lower than that of OPC, particularly for light-burned MgO (700–1000 °C compared to 1450 °C)90,91. In addition to the dry route of calcining magnesite (MgCO3) similar to OPC, magnesia resources can also be extracted from reject brine or seawater through wet processes, thereby enhancing the diversity of MgO resource acquisition92,93,94. A unique system within magnesia-based binders is carbonated reactive magnesia cement (RMC), which enables the sequestration of CO2 in building materials95,96,97, offering a crucial technological pathway for reducing carbon emissions in the construction industry. Optimizing the performance of magnesia-based materials while further minimizing their carbon footprint represents a key area of future development for this system.

The development of LC3, an innovative ternary cementitious system, arises from the constraints on the extent to which SCMs can replace OPC98,99,100. The primary reaction in LC3 involves the interaction between alumina in calcined clay and carbonate in limestone, augmented by the inherent pozzolanic activity of the calcined clay and the physical filling effect provided by limestone. Considering the global abundance of clay and limestone, the feasibility of producing and manufacturing LC3 on a worldwide scale is well-supported. Previous studies101,102,103,104 have demonstrated that clays from various regions can be used to produce LC3 with excellent mechanical properties. While 95% of the clinker in the OPC system is associated with carbon emissions from raw materials and fuels, LC3 reduces this proportion to 50% and requires 20% less thermal energy in the calcination process, highlighting its significant low-carbon potential105. Figure 2 illustrates a hybrid ML and multi-objective optimization (MOO) framework for LC3 concrete mix design106. Curated LC3 data are preprocessed and modeled for strength prediction using MICE-XGBoost, with Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis employed to interpret key influencing parameters. The trained model is then integrated with non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) to generate Pareto-optimal mixtures that balance cost and embodied CO2, achieving simultaneous reductions of approximately 13% in cost and 15% in embodied carbon at target strength levels.

Overall, Table 2 summarizes recent applications of ML in the three alternative-binder systems discussed above. While the majority of studies primarily focused on using various ML models to predict CS, there was also literature (e.g., refs. 107,108,109,110) that emphasized the early performance of these alternative systems, particularly rheology. Furthermore, another study (ref.111) employed an ML algorithm to predict the degree of hydration and carbonation in samples, utilizing interpretability algorithms such as Partial Dependence Plots (PDP) and SHAP to analyze the correlation between input and output parameters. A review of the studies summarized in Table 2 shows that ML applications in alternative binders not only enhance predictive accuracy but also uncover system-specific reaction mechanisms and governing parameters. For AAMs, ensemble models such as GB and RF effectively identified the dominant influence of curing age, activator modulus, and aggregate content on strength and rheology, while feature-importance analyses linked sodium silicate dosage to both CO2 emissions and rheological evolution. In magnesia-based binders, interpretable ML models (e.g., SHAP and PDP) revealed how carbonation duration, CO2 concentration, and w/b ratio jointly control hydration and carbonation kinetics, thus providing quantitative insights unattainable by conventional empirical methods. For LC3 systems, ML-assisted optimization has been used to fine-tune limestone and calcined-clay proportions under strength and durability constraints, illustrating the potential for carbon-aware mixture design. Representative studies have also coupled ML prediction with MOO for alternative binders, whereas broader optimization frameworks and trade-off analyses across concrete systems are discussed later in the Discussion.

ML-based mix-design optimization reduces reliance on trial-and-error experimentation and enables systematic trade-off evaluation among performance, cost, and embodied carbon, thereby supporting more sustainable concrete mixture design112,113,114,115,116.

Several studies have demonstrated the potential of ML-assisted optimization to balance mechanical performance and sustainability objectives. Naseri et al.117 proposed a data pruning strategy combined with meta-heuristic optimization algorithms to identify concrete mixtures that achieve acceptable strength while improving sustainability indicators. Their results showed that mixtures with the highest CS often exhibit inferior sustainability performance due to elevated cement and admixture contents, whereas alternative designs provide more balanced trade-offs. These findings highlight the importance of optimization frameworks that explicitly consider environmental criteria, rather than relying solely on strength-based selection.

Shahrokhishahraki et al.118 utilized ANN and several regression-based ML algorithms, including Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), Extra Trees, and Elastic Net, to optimize the concrete mix design for structural elements targeting 90-day full strength. Among these models, the ANN and regression approaches achieved prediction accuracies of 94% and 90%, respectively. The Elastic Net algorithm119, which combines L1 (lasso) and L2 (ridge) regularization terms to improve generalization and mitigate overfitting, exhibited the best performance in predicting and optimizing cement content, leading to approximately 10% reductions in both cement consumption and CO2 emissions in a mid-sized reinforced concrete case study.

For high-performance systems, particularly ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC), the relationship between strength and embodied carbon becomes increasingly critical. Due to its high cement content, UHPC typically exhibits higher volumetric CO2 emissions than conventional concrete120,121. ML-based studies have shown that mixtures achieving similar strength levels can differ substantially in embodied carbon depending on composition122. Cement content remains the dominant contributor to UHPC carbon intensity, and ML-enabled assessment reveals an approximately exponential increase in embodied carbon with increasing strength. However, system-level analyses indicate that high-strength concretes are not inherently unsustainable. When evaluated at the structural or life-cycle level, reduced cross-sectional dimensions, lower material volumes, and decreased reinforcement demand can offset higher volumetric emissions, leading to improved overall eco-efficiency123. These findings suggest that decision-making based solely on unit-volume carbon metrics may be misleading for infrastructure-scale applications.

To address multiple, often competing design objectives, ML models have increasingly been coupled with MOO frameworks. For UHPC, predictive models constrained by strength, workability, and mixture proportions have been combined with GAs to minimize carbon emissions while satisfying performance requirements124. Similarly, data-driven optimization of high-strength concrete has demonstrated that sustainable mixtures with CS exceeding 70 MPa can be achieved with reduced cement content through the judicious use of superplasticizers and SCMs125. Rather than identifying a single optimal mixture, tri-objective optimization frameworks incorporating CS, cost, and cement consumption generate Pareto-optimal solution sets, enabling designers to transparently evaluate trade-offs among mechanical performance, economic cost, and carbon emissions and to support informed, carbon-aware mix design decisions, while recognizing that the magnitude of these differences may be influenced by practical variability in mix composition and material sourcing.

The application of statistical and ML methods to predict the CS of concrete based on mixture proportions has shown promise in enhancing concrete mixture design, quality control, and quality assurance. A previous study126 utilizing a dataset of over 10,000 CS measurements from a vertically integrated cement/concrete producer revealed that while the models demonstrated high predictive accuracy for laboratory samples, their effectiveness was reduced for on-site data due to uncontrolled field variability. Despite this, predictions maintained an average relative error of less than 10%. Furthermore, an ANN-based optimization procedure was developed to minimize costs and embodied CO2 for target strength mixtures, demonstrating the potential of data-driven approaches to optimize concrete production, reduce material waste, and design cost-efficient and sustainable mixtures.

In addition to the studies discussed above, several other representative studies employing multi-objective optimization for concrete mix design are summarized in Table 3. Building on these approaches, hybrid ML–optimization frameworks have been developed to support durability-oriented mix design under realistic engineering conditions. By coupling RF models with the NSGA-II, studies have simultaneously predicted durability indicators and optimized mix proportions for infrastructure applications127. When applied to a cold-region expressway project, these frameworks enabled the identification of concrete mixtures with enhanced frost resistance and reduced chloride permeability at controlled cost levels, demonstrating their potential to guide performance- and durability-driven mix design in practice. Rather than serving as solely predictive tools, such integrated frameworks illustrate how ML can be embedded into engineering decision-making to address durability, cost, and sustainability objectives concurrently.

The US Environmental Protection Agency defines construction and demolition waste (CDW) as waste generated during new construction activities, as well as the renovation or demolition of existing structures128. Common examples of CDW include waste concrete, asphalt, bricks, gypsum, metal, and other materials129. Proper disposal of CDW has been a longstanding concern, as it often does not decompose naturally through methods like landfilling. Additionally, since CDW may contain heavy metals that pose health risks, improper disposal can, in extreme cases, result in groundwater contamination.

The concept of RAC stems from the initiative to recycle CDW, offering considerable environmental and economic benefits130. A life cycle assessment of recycled coarse aggregate (RCA) has shown that using coarse aggregates recycled from CDW can reduce carbon emissions by 65% and decrease non-renewable energy consumption by 58%131. Despite the significant sustainability potential of RAC, its mechanical properties are typically weaker than those of concrete made with natural aggregates, which has significantly limited its widespread adoption. Consequently, the relatively low strength of RAC has highlighted the urgent need to enhance its performance through optimizing RCA properties, mix design, and other influencing factors.

Numerous studies have applied ML algorithms to predict the CS of RAC, addressing the variability introduced by recycled aggregates. Khan et al.132 evaluated DT, GB, and bagging regressors, demonstrating that ensemble-based models provide superior predictive accuracy for RAC strength. Building on predictive modeling, Peng and Unluer6 employed interpretable ML techniques, including PDP and SHAP analysis, to identify cement content, water content, natural fine aggregate proportion, and water absorption as the dominant variables governing RAC mechanical performance. Pal et al.133 further extended ML applications to fiber-reinforced rubberized recycled aggregate concrete (FR3C), where advanced ensemble models achieved high prediction accuracy and revealed the critical influence of w/b ratio, aggregate size, and rubber content on CS.

Beyond CS, ML models have been successfully applied to predict additional performance attributes of RAC. Han et al.134 developed an ensemble ML framework to estimate the modulus of elasticity (MOE), demonstrating that optimized combinations of w/b ratio, RCA content, and water absorption can achieve high stiffness levels. Similarly, ML-based surrogate models have shown strong capability in predicting RAC creep behavior, with feature-importance analyses consistently identifying loading age, water absorption, and strength-related parameters as key influencing factors135. These studies highlight the versatility of ML in capturing both short-term and time-dependent mechanical behavior in RAC systems.

The aforementioned studies largely focus on predicting individual performance attributes of RAC. In contrast, Wang et al.136 proposed a multi-objective mix proportion optimization framework that simultaneously considered CS, chloride resistance, environmental impact, and life-cycle cost. Using a database of 807 RAC samples, their study identified cement and water content as the dominant factors influencing both strength and durability performance, and employed a combined WOA-BPNN and TOPSIS approach to evaluate trade-offs among competing objectives. FA was highlighted as an effective SCM capable of improving mechanical and durability performance without substantially increasing environmental burden or life-cycle cost.

Similarly, another study137 integrated ML with metaheuristic optimization to address the complexity of RAC mix design by jointly modeling CS, chloride permeability, and carbonation depth. The results demonstrated that low-carbon RAC mixtures can achieve substantial CO2 reductions at higher target strength levels (40-70 MPa), albeit at increased cost, whereas simultaneously achieving low-carbon and cost-effective solutions becomes more challenging at lower strength levels (20-30 MPa). The analysis further revealed that low-carbon mixtures generally require higher SCM-to-binder ratios, particularly for target strengths above 40 MPa, while cost-driven designs favor lower SCM contents across durability requirements. These findings highlight the necessity of multi-objective decision frameworks for balancing performance, cost, and carbon emissions in RAC applications.

Machine learning has demonstrated significant capability in predicting and optimizing the properties of RAC. By modeling complex relationships among mix composition, aggregate quality, and curing conditions, ML enables accurate estimation of strength, stiffness, and shrinkage. Feature-importance and sensitivity analyses clarify how parameters such as w/b ratio, aggregate replacement rate, and water absorption influence performance, and indicate that recycled aggregates may also affect the carbon intensity of concrete depending on mixture design and material quality. Moreover, ML-assisted MOO provides a practical pathway for designing low-carbon, high-performance RAC mixtures, advancing both material efficiency and sustainability in concrete recycling.

Lifecycle relevance of ML in low-carbon concrete

The previous sections have reviewed recent applications of machine learning in support of lower-carbon cement and concrete across multiple stages of the material lifecycle, including raw material production, mixture design, and the development of more sustainable concrete systems. Taken together, these studies indicate that ML can provide a useful decision-support framework for reducing energy demand, limiting material inefficiencies, and, in some cases, lowering associated CO2 emissions. Its value therefore lies not only in prediction itself, but also in its capacity to inform material selection, process control, and mixture design.

In cement production, ML-based models have been used to monitor and optimize key process variables in clinker manufacture. By capturing nonlinear interactions among operational parameters, these models can improve process control under industrial conditions that are inherently variable and uncertain. Because emissions from cement production arise from both calcination and energy use related to fuel combustion and electricity consumption138,139, recent work has also highlighted the value of data-driven approaches based on electricity-use data, which are often more stable and accessible than direct point-source emission measurements. Such approaches may therefore provide a more consistent basis for emission estimation and process-level optimization, although their reliability will still depend on plant-specific conditions and data quality.

At the concrete scale, ML has shown clear potential in mixture design when performance and sustainability must be considered simultaneously. Applications ranging from compressive-strength prediction to carbon-aware optimization show that ML-based frameworks can reduce reliance on iterative trial-and-error testing and support more efficient use of cementitious materials. The coupling of ML with multi-objective optimization is particularly important in this context, as it enables explicit evaluation of trade-offs among strength, durability, cost, and environmental impact. In this way, the role of ML extends beyond property prediction alone toward more transparent and practically relevant decision-making. Figure 3 summarizes this transition from prediction-oriented modeling to decision support in low-carbon cement and concrete, while also highlighting the associated limitations and future development needs.

Data limitations and model generalizability

Despite these encouraging developments, several factors still limit the broader uptake of ML in cementitious materials research and engineering practice. A persistent difficulty lies in the availability, quality, and representativeness of data. Many published models are trained on relatively small datasets generated under controlled laboratory conditions and therefore do not fully reflect the variability inherent in construction practice. As previous studies have shown, models that perform well for laboratory-prepared samples often exhibit reduced accuracy when applied to field data, where factors such as water content, curing conditions, aggregate characteristics, admixture efficiency, and testing procedures are less tightly controlled140.

These constraints directly affect the generalizability and reliability of ML-based predictions. Laboratory datasets remain valuable for identifying trends and establishing initial structure-property relationships, but direct transfer of such models to site conditions is not straightforward. Improving robustness will therefore require broader datasets that incorporate field measurements, together with input variables that better represent environmental exposure, material variability, and operational uncertainty.

It should also be noted that high predictive accuracy, considered in isolation, does not explain why a particular algorithm performs well for a given cementitious system. Ensemble-learning approaches, including RF and GB methods, often show strong performance because they are well suited to capturing nonlinear interactions among compositional, processing, and curing variables. However, the apparent superiority of one algorithm over another is often contingent on the nature of the dataset and the material system under study, rather than indicating any generally preferred model form.

A related challenge concerns transferability across different binder systems. Models developed for OPC-based concretes cannot be assumed to remain valid for LC3, AAMs, or recycled-material-based systems, because the governing reaction mechanisms and pathways of microstructural development differ substantially among these materials. This is one reason why the literature often shows inconsistencies in both model ranking and feature importance. Recent studies suggest that better transferability may require feature representations more closely connected to the underlying physico-chemical processes of the binder, including chemistry-informed descriptors such as oxide composition and phase assemblage, as well as microstructure-related variables such as porosity and pore-network development. Progress in this area will depend not only on larger datasets, but also on descriptors that more faithfully represent binder chemistry, exposure conditions, and the evolution of material structure over time.

Interpretability and risks of data-driven models

A further limitation is inherent in the way many ML models are constructed. Because they are driven primarily by statistical relationships within the available dataset, there is no guarantee that the resulting predictions will remain physically meaningful outside that domain. In cementitious systems of high compositional and chemical complexity, particularly those incorporating SCMs, alternative binders, or recycled aggregates, this becomes a non-trivial concern. Predictions may remain numerically plausible while departing from known material behavior, especially when models are applied to mixture compositions or curing conditions for which only limited experimental evidence is available.

This also affects the interpretation of model outputs. Tools such as SHAP and PDP have provided useful ways to examine variable importance and response trends, but they do not remove the need for caution in interpretation. Their outputs are influenced by assumptions embedded in the model structure, by correlations among input variables, and, in some cases, by the computational procedures used to generate the explanation itself. For this reason, such methods are best regarded as aids to analysis rather than as evidence of causality. Their value is greatest when used alongside, rather than in place of, established understanding of cement chemistry, reaction kinetics, and microstructural development.

Prediction versus carbon mitigation

A related issue is that predictive success should not be conflated with carbon mitigation. Much of the published work in this area remains focused on the prediction of strength, workability, or durability indicators, while the environmental relevance of the model is introduced only indirectly, if at all. Under such circumstances, improved predictive accuracy does not necessarily imply any meaningful reduction in embodied CO2. That outcome depends on whether the modeling framework explicitly incorporates variables and objectives linked to decarbonization, such as clinker reduction, SCM substitution, or the use of alternative binders.

If ML is to contribute more directly to low-carbon concrete development, environmental metrics need to be treated as primary design criteria rather than secondary consequences of performance prediction. This includes not only embodied carbon, but also broader lifecycle indicators where relevant. Without such integration, there is a risk that increasingly accurate models will remain analytically impressive yet only loosely connected to the central objective of emissions reduction.

Toward physically informed ML frameworks

Addressing these limitations will require a move beyond purely predictive modeling toward ML frameworks that are more closely connected to the underlying behavior of cementitious materials. One important direction is the integration of ML with physics-based approaches, including thermodynamic modeling and microstructural characterization. Such combinations can provide a degree of constraint that is often lacking in purely data-driven models, and may therefore improve both physical consistency and interpretability. The examples discussed in this review suggest that coupling ML with thermodynamic simulations or image-based microstructural analysis can be particularly useful for alternative binder systems and other low-carbon cement formulations, where purely empirical generalization is often difficult141,142.

A second requirement is that sustainability should be embedded more explicitly within the modeling framework itself. Although several recent studies have incorporated embodied carbon alongside mechanical performance, this captures only part of the broader decision space relevant to low-carbon concrete. Factors such as resource efficiency, economic feasibility, and long-term durability also need to be considered if the outputs of ML models are to be of practical value. The use of SCMs and recycled aggregates illustrates this clearly, because any environmental benefit must be evaluated alongside its consequences for performance and cost. This is likely to require multi-objective frameworks that are able to represent such trade-offs directly, rather than treating sustainability as a secondary outcome. Figure 4 outlines this broader progression, from conventional prediction toward physics-informed modeling and sustainability-oriented decision-making.

Recycled aggregates and circularity

The application of ML to RAC illustrates both the opportunities and challenges of data-driven design in circular construction. ML models have demonstrated reliable prediction of key mechanical and time-dependent properties of RAC, including CS, MOE, and creep behavior6,134,135. Beyond prediction, feature-importance analyses provide quantitative insights into how mixture parameters, such as RCA replacement rate, adhered mortar content, water absorption, and loading age, govern macroscopic performance.

More importantly, recent studies integrating ML with metaheuristic optimization algorithms highlight the role of ML in balancing performance, durability, cost, and carbon reduction in RAC design. While low-carbon mixtures may involve higher material costs, particularly at higher strength levels, they offer substantial reductions in CO2 emissions. These findings emphasize that ML contributes not merely as a predictive tool but as a means of enabling system-level decision-making that supports sustainable material use and circular economy principles.

Synthesis and outlook

The literature reviewed here suggests that the main barriers to wider use of ML in cement and concrete engineering lie in the quality and representativeness of available data, the difficulty of achieving robust generalization under field conditions, and the possibility of predictions that are statistically strong yet physically questionable. At the same time, the studies discussed in this review indicate that these limitations are not intrinsic to the use of ML itself, but may be reduced through broader inclusion of field-scale data, closer incorporation of physical constraints, and the use of multi-objective frameworks that treat sustainability-related variables explicitly.

ML should therefore not be regarded as a substitute for established materials science and engineering approaches. Its role is more appropriately seen as complementary: a means of assisting the analysis of complex relationships and supporting decisions where trade-offs among performance, cost, and environmental impact are not easily resolved by conventional methods alone. When applied within appropriate physical and engineering boundaries, ML can make a useful contribution to the development of lower-carbon and more resource-efficient cement and concrete systems.
